title_candidates: Don't Squish the 30-Legged Bug in Your Bathroom (Here's Why)
The 30-Legged Bug in Your House You Shouldn't Squish
Why a 30-Legged Bug Is Living in Your Bathroom
pinned_comment: Be honest: the last time a house centipede ran across your floor, what did you actually do? 👇
thumb: one house centipede filling the frame, low angle on the tile; text: DON'T SQUISH

The bug in the bathroom: psu: 'Adult house centipedes have 15 pairs of legs'
psu: 'House centipedes feed on silverfish, firebrats, carpet beetle larvae, cockroaches, spiders'
What's on the menu: caes: 'actively hunt other arthropods such as cockroach nymphs, bed bugs, flies, ants, silverfish, spiders'
uark: 'feed readily on cockroach nymphs, flies, moths, bedbugs, crickets, silverfish, earwigs' / 'They can capture several prey items at one time. They feed on one specimen while holding the others'
Why your bathroom: caes: 'prefer cool, humid, dark environments ... basements, cellars, and first-floor bathrooms'
psu: 'In floor drains without water traps' / 'Under and in cardboard boxes' / 'crawl spaces' / 'do not survive winters outdoors in Pennsylvania, but readily reproduce in heated structures'
The night shift: psu: 'come out at night to forage for prey'
caes: 'nocturnal and incredibly wary. Most that live in houses are never seen' / 'will immediately flee if they are discovered'
wisc: 'They hunt for prey at night and can become trapped if they fall into a sink or bathtub'
How it hunts: caes: 'fast runners that actively chase down prey' / 'forcipules (modified pincer-like legs) located directly underneath their mouthparts'
uark: 'stopping suddenly and remaining motionless for some time before racing off once more' / 'half pouncing and half lassoing' / 'well-developed, faceted eyes' unlike most other centipedes
Will it bite me?: caes: 'a house centipede stinging a human is very rare ... the result of rough handling' / 'do not cause harm to structures or to stored products, fabrics, pets, or humans'
uark: 'jaws are not powerful enough to break human skin easily' / 'in most cases the bite is no worse than the sting of a bee' (but 'Severe swelling and pain can result')
The leg trick: frontiers (2024): legs break at a preferred autotomy plane and are usually regenerated within one molting cycle (explosive regeneration)
caes: 'two antennae in front that are similar in appearance to their legs, making it difficult for potential predators to tell which way it is facing'
Why it looks so scary: psu: 'one to one and one-half inches in length ... an overall appearance of being from three to four inches in length (including legs and antennae)' / 'the last pair (on adult females) nearly twice the length of the body'
Baby centipedes: psu: 'produce up to 150 young' / 'Newly hatched larvae ... have four pairs of legs. During the next five larval molts ... 5, 7, 9, 11, and 13 pairs' then 15
caes: 'taking upwards of 3 years to reach sexual maturity'
Where it came from: psu: 'native to the Mediterranean region ... first recorded in Pennsylvania in 1849'
uark: 'It reached Pennsylvania in 1849, New York in 1885, and Massachusetts about 1890, and it now extends westward to the Rocky Mountains and beyond'
How long it lives: caes: 'can live as long as 7 years'
Getting rid of them: psu: 'If house centipedes are seen frequently, this indicates that some prey arthropod is in abundance' / 'fill or seal cracks' / 'Reduce the humidity by utilizing dehumidifiers'
caes: 'running fans or dehumidifiers. Address water issues' / 'reduces the number of hunting centipedes' / 'Using pesticides to eradicate house centipedes is not recommended'
wisc: 'there is no need for control. They are beneficial'

psu: 'Install window screens in basement floor drains' / sticky insect traps (monitors) show which arthropods are feeding the centipedes; wisc: 'Small sticky board traps can be placed in areas of activity'
The verdict: caes: 'beneficial residents that act as biocontrol against building pests'

long.t: Meatball, there's a bug with 30 legs in my bathroom.
Do I squish it?
Don't! It's eating your roaches.
...How many roaches?
Oh. / You don't want to know.
Stick around. By the end, you'll be paying it rent.
I am not paying a bug rent.
We'll see.
Okay. What else does it eat?
Spiders. Silverfish. Ants. Even bed bugs.
long.card: EATS BED BUGS TOO + SPIDERS, SILVERFISH, ANTS

long.t: Flies, moths, earwigs, crickets.
Carpet beetle larvae. Firebrats. Baby cockroaches.
And here's the wild part. It can catch several bugs at once.
long.card: CAN CATCH SEVERAL BUGS AT ONCE

long.t: It eats one, while it holds the others.
It packs a lunch?!
In its legs. Yes.
But why my bathroom?
It loves damp, dark spots. Like drains.
long.card: BATHROOMS - BASEMENTS - DRAINS / DAMP, DARK SPOTS

long.t: Especially floor drains with no water trap.
Basements. Crawl spaces. Under cardboard boxes.
Why doesn't it just live outside?
In places like Pennsylvania, it can't survive the winter outdoors.
But in a heated house? It breeds just fine.
So I'm running a bug hotel.
Five stars. Great drains.
And it works the night shift.
long.card: HUNTS AT NIGHT / HIDES IN DAMP, DARK SPOTS BY DAY

long.t: While I sleep?
You're welcome.
Flip on the light, and it's gone. It flees the second it's seen.
It's so sneaky, most of them are never seen at all.
That's worse. That is so much worse.
Well, except the ones that fall in your tub at night and get trapped.
long.card: CAN GET TRAPPED IN SINKS AND TUBS

long.t: So that's why it's in my tub every morning!
It's not stalking you. It's stuck.
How does it even catch stuff?
It's a fast runner. It chases its prey down.
When it runs, it sometimes stops dead, freezes, then races off again.
long.card: WHEN IT RUNS: STOPS, FREEZES, RACES OFF

long.t: Then it can pounce, lasso, and sting.
Stings? With what?
A pair of legs, turned into venom pincers, right under its mouth.
And unlike most centipedes, it has real compound eyes.
Venom?! Will it bite me?
Almost never. Mostly if you grab it.
long.card: STINGS ARE VERY RARE / MOSTLY FROM ROUGH HANDLING

long.t: Its jaws can barely break human skin.
Usually? About like a bee sting. It can still swell and hurt.
long.card: USUALLY ABOUT LIKE A BEE STING / CAN SWELL AND HURT

long.t: And it won't hurt your pets, your clothes, or your house.
long.card: NO HARM TO PETS, FABRICS OR BUILDINGS

long.t: Okay, but what if I do grab it?
Then you'll see its best trick.
Its leg just fell off!
Normal! It drops legs to escape.
Each leg has a built-in breaking point.
long.card: LEGS BREAK AT A BUILT-IN WEAK SPOT

long.t: And by its next molt, it usually grows the leg back.
long.card: USUALLY REGROWS IT BY THE NEXT MOLT

long.t: Can I do that?
No.
See those long things up front? Antennae. They look just like legs.
So a predator has a hard time telling which end is the head.
long.card: HARD FOR PREDATORS TO TELL WHICH WAY IT FACES

long.t: Honestly? Me neither.
Why does it look so terrifying?
Its body's about an inch to an inch and a half long.
But the legs and antennae make it look three or four inches.
And on females, the back legs can be nearly twice as long as the body.
I hate that.
Wait. Does it have babies?
One female can have up to 150.
Babies hatch with only 8 legs.
So they're spiders?
Don't tell them.
With each early molt, they add more. Ten legs. Fourteen. Eighteen. All the way to thirty.
It can take three years just to grow up.
Three years? My phone doesn't last that long.
Where's it from, anyway?
The Mediterranean.
So it's on vacation?
Permanently.
Pennsylvania by eighteen forty-nine. New York by eighteen eighty-five. Then it kept heading west.
So it's been here longer than me.
It's got seniority.
How long do they live?
Up to seven years.
Seven?! How do I make it leave?
First, a warning. If you see a lot of them...
...you may have a bigger bug problem. They go where the food is.
long.card: SEEING LOTS OF THEM = MAYBE LOTS OF PREY

long.t: So the centipede is the smoke detector.
Exactly. Don't blame the alarm.
Dry the room. Fix leaks. Move the cardboard.
long.card: RUN A FAN - FIX LEAKS - MOVE CARDBOARD OFF SLABS

long.t: Run a dehumidifier. Seal up the cracks.
Put screens over basement floor drains.
And sticky traps will show you what it's been eating.
long.card: STICKY TRAPS SHOW WHAT IT EATS

long.t: Fewer bugs to eat means fewer centipedes.
And skip the bug spray. One state lab says there's little need.
long.card: LITTLE NEED FOR BUG SPRAY INDOORS (CT LAB)

long.t: So. Squish it, or keep it?
Keep it. It's free pest control, working nights.
long.card: VERDICT: KEEP IT / FREE PEST CONTROL

long.t: Fine. It stays. But it pays rent.
It does. In roaches.
Told you.
